analysis.investment_thesis: Chennai Petroleum is a commodity refiner with collapsed profitability: FY25 EBIT of only INR 1,016 Cr against EV of ~INR 18,447 Cr yields 5.5% earnings yield — below my threshold — and ROCE of a dismal 4.3% means the business is destroying value relative to its cost of capital. Both Magic Formula metrics fail, and the earnings trend is sharply deteriorating.
key_strengths: Debt has been aggressively repaid: borrowings fell from INR 9,167 Cr (FY21) to INR 1,933 Cr (FY25)
OCF was positive all 5 recent years, showing the refinery does generate operating cash even in weak-margin environments
Subsidiary of Indian Oil Corporation — implicit state support and secure crude supply access
key_risks: Earnings are entirely at the mercy of gross refining margins (GRMs), which swung from INR 5,698 Cr EBIT (FY23) to INR 1,016 Cr (FY25) — an 82% collapse in two years
ROCE of 4.3% and ROE of 2.5% in FY25 indicate the business is not earning its cost of capital at current refining spreads
No pricing power: product prices are linked to import parity and government policy; company is a price-taker in both crude input and product output
red_flags: Net profit collapsed from INR 3,532 Cr (FY23) to INR 214 Cr (FY25) — a 94% earnings decline in two years
Operating income CAGR over 9 years is -3.1% — the business has not grown real earnings at all despite revenue growth
ROCE of 4.3% is far below the 20% Magic Formula minimum; this is a structurally low-return commodity business
analysis.detailed_analysis: Chennai Petroleum is precisely the type of company the Magic Formula is designed to avoid: a capital-intensive commodity business that earns low returns on capital and has no control over its own economics. The FY23 boom (INR 3,532 Cr net profit) was a function of post-COVID GRM supercycle, not sustainable competitive advantage — FY25 net profit of just INR 214 Cr confirms this. On current earnings, the earnings yield is 5.5%, which doesn't compensate for the commodity risk. ROCE of 4.3% is roughly what you'd earn in a fixed deposit. There is no Magic Formula case here: the refining business has shown it cannot consistently earn above its cost of capital.
